site.title: OBT Consultant Development Track
site.tagline: An initiative of SIL Global's Consulting Pool, raising up consultants for oral Bible translation: formed in community, certified by competency.
site.footerNote: The OBT Consultant Development Track is an initiative of SIL Global's Consulting Pool, carried out with participants and partners from across the Bible translation movement. Certification follows SIL's Competency-Based Consulting standard.

pages.title: OBT Consultant Development Track
pages.metaDescription: The OBT Consultant Development Track raises up certified consultants for oral Bible translation through genre-based workshops, mentorship, and competency-based certification.

blocks.title: Consultants for a Bible that lives out loud
blocks.body:
Oral Bible translation is growing faster than any form of Bible translation ever has. The consultants who safeguard its quality are still far too few.

The OBT Consultant Development Track forms and certifies consultants for this work: in community, through real practice, at the pace of genuine readiness.

blocks.title: Certification that follows readiness, not seat time
blocks.body:
This track certifies oral Bible translation consultants when they demonstrate the full set of consulting competencies, wherever and however they gained them.

We call it the roundabout model. Instead of a fixed sequence of required courses, the track is a circulation: people enter from different directions, keep moving while they grow, and exit when a mentor confirms they are ready.

blocks.title: Training is usually drawn as a straight road
blocks.body:
Attend the courses in order, pass the milestones, arrive at certification. A straight road works well when everyone starts from the same place and can travel on the same schedule.

OBT consultants do not start from the same place. They come from many nations and ministries, carry very different training histories, and most are already serving translation projects they cannot simply leave for a year of coursework.

blocks.title: So we built a roundabout
blocks.body:
A roundabout has many entry roads. A field translator with years of experience, an exegete from a partner organization, a consultant adding an oral specialization: each enters from where they actually are, usually through our experiential OBT crash course or equivalent experience.

No one is sent back to the start of someone else's road. And no one has to stop serving their projects in order to keep moving.

blocks.title: On the roundabout, five threads weave together
blocks.body:
Circulating means growing along five threads at once: genre-based workshops that act as catalysts, online trainings between them, biblical language cohorts, ongoing mentorship, and supervised practice on real translation projects.

Every lap adds evidence. A workshop evaluation here, a mentored consultant check there, a language milestone, a teaching assignment. The track keeps that evidence, competency by competency.

blocks.title: Progress you can actually see
blocks.body:
Every workshop activity is tied to specific, observable competencies. Multiple facilitators record what they see each participant do, then translate those observations into simple 0 to 3 ratings against SIL's Competency-Based Consulting matrix.

Because many evaluators watch many activities over weeks of intense collaboration, the picture is rich and hard to fake, and it is verified by the facilitators before anything enters a participant's record.

blocks.title: The exit is readiness, confirmed by a mentor
blocks.body:
Workshop scores never certify anyone. Each participant has a consultant-mentor who walks with them, weighs all the evidence, and confirms when the full competency set is genuinely in place. That confirmation is the exit ramp.

Some people exit after a few laps; others circulate longer. On a roundabout, that is not falling behind. It is how the model is supposed to work.

blocks.title: And the roundabout keeps turning
blocks.body:
The first cycle aims to certify 25 OBT-specialized consultants. But graduates do not simply drive away: strong participants return as session leaders, mentors, and workshop facilitators for the next generation.

The goal is not one cohort of consultants. It is a sustainable, replicable pathway that regions can carry forward themselves.

blocks.title: Walk the loop yourself
blocks.body: The pages below unpack each part of the model: why the track exists, how certification works, and what the five threads look like in practice.

pages.title: Why this track exists
pages.metaDescription: Oral Bible translation has grown explosively, and the consultants who safeguard its quality are scarce. Why the OBT Consultant Development Track was built, and the principles that shape it.

blocks.title: The fastest growth Bible translation has ever seen
blocks.body:
In roughly 120 years, written Bible translation grew from about 10 active projects to about 800. Oral Bible translation grew from about 20 active projects to more than 1,200 in six years.

The reason is impact. In an OBT project, a team of mature believers internalizes long sections of Scripture and translates them from memory, orally, into the heart language of their community. By the time a book is finished, the community has orally processed every passage many times over.
These translators end up holding entire books of the Bible in memory. In their communities, they are often called walking Bibles.
blocks.attribution: Why OBT projects multiply so quickly

blocks.title: Growth has outrun quality assurance
blocks.body:
Every Bible translation project needs consultants: experienced practitioners who check the translation with the team so that what the community receives is accurate, clear, and natural. OBT projects have multiplied faster than the consulting pool can sustain, and the pool of consultants equipped to evaluate specifically oral translation meets only a small fraction of the need.

There is a deeper problem than headcount. Nearly all existing consultant training was built around literacy: written commentaries, written drafts, written feedback. Oral Bible translation follows an oral method and produces an oral product, so its consultants need a substantially different repertoire of analytical, relational, and intuitive skills.

blocks.title: Four realities shape the whole curriculum

items.title: Performance carries meaning
items.body: Intonation, pacing, and emotional expression all bear on whether a translation communicates faithfully. Consultants must evaluate dimensions of meaning that never appear in a written back translation.

items.title: Genre drives the challenges
items.body: Checking a narrative means attending to story flow and participant reference; checking a psalm means understanding Hebrew poetics and local artistic genres. The skills differ so much by genre that the whole workshop series is organized around genres.

items.title: Contexts vary enormously
items.body: Some consultants work face to face with community performers; others work virtually with teams in restricted-access areas. Different workflows and checking technologies place very different demands on the consultant.

items.title: Consultants serve many languages
items.body: Most OBT consultants serve multiple language communities without deep knowledge of any single one, so training focuses on transferable analytical frameworks and consulting postures rather than language-specific knowledge.

blocks.caption: Meaning in oral translation lives in performance: voice, pacing, expression, and local art forms.

blocks.title: Three principles decide what we teach
blocks.body: Everything in the track flows from a single commitment: start with orality, and design everything else around it. Three working principles carry that commitment into each workshop.

items.title: Teach what cannot be gained elsewhere
items.body: Excellent resources already cover biblical languages, linguistics, and Bible background, and we point participants to them. Precious in-person time goes to what those resources do not provide: OBT-specific exegesis, oral genre discovery, checking practice, and the formation of a consulting identity.

items.title: Practice first, theory layered on
items.body: Participants exegete, internalize, draft, revise, and prepare for checking inside every workshop, with corrective feedback at each step. Having wrestled with a genre from the inside, they can later speak into its challenges with earned authority.

items.title: Model the methods consultants will use
items.body: The workshops deliberately teach through oral, experiential, discussion-based methods that participants can turn around and use with their own translation teams, rather than defaulting to lecture.

pages.title: How certification works
pages.metaDescription: The OBT-CDT certifies consultants through the Competency-Based Consulting method: observable evidence, a 0 to 3 rubric, multiple evaluators, and a mentor who confirms readiness.

blocks.title: Competency-based consulting in plain terms
blocks.body:
SIL maintains a matrix of the competencies a Bible translation consultant needs: exegesis, discourse analysis, consulting process skills, interpersonal skills, technology, and more. Competency-Based Consulting (CBC) is the discipline of certifying people against that matrix using documented evidence, rather than against a list of courses attended.

The track is built on the method itself. The particular platform that stores the records may evolve, but the discipline stays the same: name the competency, observe real behavior, document the evidence, and let a mentor weigh it.

blocks.title: From observation to evidence
blocks.body:
Before each workshop, every lesson and activity is tied to specific knowledge, skills, and attitudes (KSAs), each connected to observable phenomena, so evaluators know exactly what to watch and listen for.

During the workshop, facilitators record descriptive notes on what they actually see each participant do. Observations from multiple facilitators across many activities come together in one structured record per participant, which makes the resulting picture far richer than any single observer could produce.

blocks.title: Observations become simple 0 to 3 ratings
blocks.body: Qualitative observation comes first; the numbers summarize it. Each rating is tied to a specific competency sub-point and is reviewed by facilitators who verify that it reflects what they saw.

items.label: Not yet observed
items.body: No evidence for this competency yet. A starting point, not a judgment.

items.label: Emerging
items.body: Early evidence is present; the participant needs substantial support in this area.

items.label: Developing
items.body: Solid, repeated evidence; the participant works well with light support.

items.label: Established
items.body: Consistent, independent competence, confirmed across activities and evaluators.

blocks.body: A workshop is both a fishbowl and a pressure cooker. Across weeks of intense multicultural teamwork, real strengths and real growth areas both come clearly into view.

items.title: Continuous observation
items.body: Facilitators watch and note evidence throughout activities, tagged to the participant or group it belongs to.

items.title: Processing the day
items.body: The facilitation team reviews and consolidates the day's observations while they are fresh.

items.title: Holistic written evaluation
items.body: Each participant receives a written evaluation, drafted from the shared record and verified by multiple facilitators.

items.title: Evidence enters the record
items.body: Verified evidence is submitted into the participant's competency record, organized so their mentor can see what was observed, at what level, and by whom.

blocks.title: The mentor decides
blocks.body:
Workshop scores are evidence, never a verdict. Each participant's consultant-mentor talks the evidence through with them, weighs it alongside field experience, and assigns the final ratings at their own discretion. Certification happens when the mentor confirms the full competency set is in place.

This is what makes the roundabout model trustworthy: the track generates unusually rich, verified evidence, and a human being who knows the participant makes the call.

pages.title: The Five Threads
pages.metaDescription: Five interlocking threads form OBT consultants: genre-based workshops, online trainings, biblical language cohorts, ongoing mentorship, and field-based application.

blocks.title: Formation woven from five threads
blocks.body:
Competency development in the track is distributed across five interlocking threads. Together they provide training and mentorship sufficient to meet the full set of consulting competencies.

Participants are not expected to engage every thread in equal measure. Each person draws most heavily on the threads that will most effectively advance their own readiness, which is exactly what the roundabout model is for.

items.title: Workshops as catalysts
items.body: Five two-week intensives, each centered on a major biblical genre: Narrative, Epistles, Psalms, Legal Texts in the Torah, and Prophecy and Wisdom Literature. Participants practice most consulting competencies inside the genre at hand, with feedback at every step.

items.title: Online trainings
items.body: Between workshops, live virtual sessions target the competencies the previous workshop showed participants most need, alongside curated self-paced material. Wherever possible these run with cohort elements, so no one studies alone.

items.title: Biblical language cohorts
items.body: Participants build Hebrew and Greek competence through structured coursework with guidance from a biblical-language mentor, cohort-style. The workshops apply that knowledge to oral translation; the cohorts build the foundation.

items.title: Ongoing mentorship
items.body: Each consultant-in-training works with an assigned consultant-mentor who monitors development, guides growth, and ultimately validates readiness for certification, supported by feedback from many consultants and subject-matter experts along the way.

items.title: Field-based application
items.body: Participants observe practicing OBT consultants and conduct supervised consultant checks on real translation projects. Strong participants are also trained to lead crash-course sessions for the next round, deepening mastery by teaching.

blocks.title: The workshops are the visible thread, not the whole fabric
blocks.body:
Workshops act as catalysts: two weeks that ignite skills and expose exactly where each participant should grow next. But the track depends equally on what happens between them: the virtual sessions, the language cohorts, the mentor conversations, and the supervised checks on real projects.

Evaluation data from each workshop feeds directly into what gets taught between workshops, so the track adapts to the actual cohort rather than to a fixed syllabus.

blocks.caption: Cohorts keep participants moving together between workshops.

pages.title: The workshop series
pages.metaDescription: Five two-week, genre-based workshops anchor the OBT Consultant Development Track: Narrative, Epistles, Psalms, Legal Texts in the Torah, and Prophecy and Wisdom Literature.

blocks.title: Every workshop follows the same arc
blocks.body:
Each workshop moves through genre-specific instruction, hands-on translation experience, and supervised consulting practice. Participants exegete, internalize, draft, revise, and check within the two weeks, so competencies are practiced rather than merely presented.

The series progresses from more accessible genres toward more complex ones, and the one-week experiential OBT Crash Course is the recommended doorway for newcomers: each crash-course participant learns oral Bible translation by doing it, functioning as a mother-tongue translator for a week.

items.title: 1 · Narrative — Bangalore, India
items.body: Foundational OBT translation skills, OBT-specific exegesis, internalization, and introductory consulting awareness.

items.title: 2 · Epistles — Chiang Mai, Thailand
items.body: Argument structure and prominence in the Epistles, with structured consulting practice on a real OBT translation.

items.title: 3 · Psalms — Bali, Indonesia
items.body: Hebrew poetry exegesis for OBT and the facilitation of Psalms translation into local artistic genres.

items.title: 4 · Legal Texts in the Torah
items.body: Legal and sacrificial codes in the Torah and the genre-specific consulting challenges they present.

items.title: 5 · Prophecy and Wisdom Literature
items.body: Prophetic and wisdom literature, and consolidation of the full consulting skill set. Prophecy follows the legal texts because it so often depends on the Torah's covenantal material.

blocks.title: Single-workshop visits are genuinely welcome
blocks.body: Visiting one workshop is an effective way to assess whether the track fits a mentee, to add an oral specialization to an existing consulting certification, or to contribute as a session leader or evaluator.

pages.title: Help form the next OBT consultants
pages.metaDescription: The OBT Consultant Development Track needs OBT consultant-mentors, mentors in linguistics and biblical languages, checking opportunities on real projects, and sponsorship partners.

blocks.title: A track like this runs on people who give their skill away
blocks.body:
Our participants are capable, motivated, and already serving oral Bible translation projects across more than eight nations. What stands between many of them and certification is not ability. It is access: to mentors, to supervised practice, and to the kind of sustained relationships that form consultants.

If you carry experience in Bible translation consulting, linguistics, or the biblical languages, there is a concrete place for you here.

items.title: Mentor as an OBT consultant
items.body: Our most pressing need. Practicing OBT consultants who will take on one or more consultants-in-training: monitoring their development, guiding their growth, and ultimately confirming their readiness for certification.

items.title: Mentor in linguistics or biblical languages
items.body: Participants build linguistics and Hebrew or Greek competence through guided self-study and cohorts. Mentors in these disciplines answer questions, review progress, and keep cohorts moving with encouragement and accountability.

items.title: Open a checking opportunity
items.body: If you lead or advise an OBT project, hosting a supervised consultant check gives a consultant-in-training the real practice they cannot get any other way, under the eye of an experienced consultant, at no cost to your project's quality.

items.title: Sponsor and partner
items.body: Most participants serve with organizations of limited means, and the track actively seeks partners to keep workshops affordable for them. Sponsorship conversations, large or small, are warmly welcome.

blocks.title: Who you would be serving
blocks.body: The current cohort is drawn from over eight nations, and most participants serve with Asian organizations of limited means. They are field translators, exegetes, and translation advisors who bring years of real project experience and are pressing toward the consulting competencies their movements urgently need.

blocks.title: Start the conversation
blocks.body: Write a few lines about who you are and how you hope to contribute, and we will follow up personally.

blocks.title: Psalms in Bali: participant handbook
blocks.body: Everything you need in order to arrive ready: what the weeks hold, where the base is, what to put in your bag, and what to do before you fly.

items.label: What you will be able to do

blocks.title: Welcome to Workshop 3
blocks.body:
The Psalter has been the church's most sustained song-and-prayer text for as long as there has been a church. Where Christians have received it as living song, in the musical forms their community already trusts with its most serious speech, it has shaped their theology and their emotional life. Where it has arrived as prose on a page, much less has happened.

Workshop 3 is about that gap. Over these weeks you will exegete Psalms 1 and 13 closely, work alongside mother-tongue translators and artists to craft them in local genres, and then check that work the way a consultant checks aesthetic Scripture.
blocks.caption: Canang sari, the daily woven offerings of flowers and petals set out across Bali.

items.label: Workshop thesis
items.title: The Psalms serve communities most fully when they are translated faithfully into artistic forms local people embrace and use, devotionally and congregationally.
What we are asking of each other

items.label: Listen closely to Scripture, to artists, to translators and to one another.
Practise consultant skills in real cross-cultural team settings.
Connect exegesis, internalisation, artistic translation and community use.
Grow through mentor guidance, peer feedback and reflective practice.
Participation

blocks.title: How the weeks build
blocks.caption: A candi bentar, the split gate that marks the entrance to a Balinese temple.

items.label: 18 to 22 August
items.body: OBT orientation and crash course: a shared starting point for people arriving from very different backgrounds.

items.label: Week one
items.body: Aesthetic language and ethnopoetics, genre in the Psalms and in cultures, the CLAT process, and hands-on crafting of Psalms 1 and 13 with artists.

items.label: Week two
items.body: Community checking, consultant checking, supervised consulting practice, and peer feedback on all of it.

items.label: Final day
items.body: Integration conversations with artists and community leaders, performances of both psalms, and the closing ceremony.

items.title: Which psalms
items.body: The workshop works closely with Psalm 1, a wisdom psalm, and Psalm 13, a lament. Hebrew poetic conventions beyond those two get their own session, so what you learn transfers to the rest of the Psalter.

items.label: Working plan
items.title: The sequence is set; the clock is not
items.body: Daily hours, meal times, where the devotionals sit, room assignments and the final facilitator roster are still being fixed. The shape below is settled.

items.title: The daily rhythm
items.body:
Mornings are theory and skill. Afternoons are application with the mother-tongue translation teams and the artists, and they are also where most competencies get observed and evaluated. Expect around seven hours of classroom time a day, with evening homework kept to about ninety minutes on average.

Each morning opens with a devotional chosen for that day's work rather than as a generic opener.

items.label: Day 1
items.body: Opening session and structured introductions between the consultant teams and the artist and translator teams. Aesthetic language and ethnopoetics in the Bible; genre in the Psalms and in cultures. Afternoon: mapping the genre repertoire of the communities present.

items.label: Day 2
items.body: CLAT overview, with Scripture goals, genre matching and genre feature analysis. Afternoon: the same three applied to Psalm 1.

items.label: Day 3
items.body: Translating aesthetic language, CLAT step 5, then Psalm 1 exegesis and an internalisation plan. Afternoon: facilitating internalisation and beginning to craft Psalm 1 as local art.

items.label: Day 4
items.body: Debrief of the Psalm 1 process, then Psalm 13 exegesis and internalisation. Afternoon: refine Psalm 1, match a genre for Psalm 13, begin crafting.

items.label: Day 5
items.body: Hebrew poetic conventions beyond Psalms 1 and 13, and how to use the Scriptura materials. Afternoon: Psalm 1 refinement and group work on Psalm 13.

items.label: Day 1
items.body: Community checking and consultant checking of artistic translations, moving into application mid-morning. Afternoon: helping the teams begin community checking of Psalm 1.

items.label: Day 2
items.body: Preparing consulting questions and a checking plan for Psalm 1, with real planning time built in. Afternoon: the consultant check itself, then revision.

items.label: Day 3
items.body: A full day of checking and revising Psalm 13, carrying on Psalm 1 work where it is needed.

items.label: Day 4
items.body: Still being decided between two options: Proverbs, or practice at being a Psalms ambassador to community leaders.

items.label: Day 5
items.body: Integration conversations and APPLY conversations with the artists in the morning. Afternoon: finalising integration plans, each group performing Psalms 1 and 13, and the closing ceremony.

blocks.title: What you will be able to do
blocks.caption: Bamboo keys of a Balinese tingklik, struck with padded mallets.

items.body: Work through a psalm deeply yourself, recognise the features of Hebrew poetry that matter for translation, and be able to say what those forms did socially and theologically in their own setting.
Ask culturally appropriate questions to find out what a community actually sings, chants and performs, then analyse the function and features of both psalm genres and candidate local ones.
Lead a contextualised version of the CLAT conversations, holding fidelity to the source and excellence in the target genre at the same time.
Prepare questions suited to aesthetic content, then take a checking conversation from spotting an issue through to resolving it.
Show community leaders inductively why a psalm in a local art form is still a faithful translation, and help artists and translators plan for it to be used.

items.title: When to arrive
items.body:
If you are joining the crash course, plan to be in Bali on Monday 17 August, during the afternoon. If you are coming only for the Psalms workshop, be on the base by Sunday 23 August.

You are very welcome to come a couple of days early and stay at the base beforehand. We especially encourage that for anyone crossing four or five time zones or more. A day or two lets your body catch up so you can work properly from the first session instead of pushing through jet lag.

items.title: When to leave
items.body: The workshop ends at 5:00 PM on Friday 4 September. Choose a late-evening flight that day, or leave on the 5th or later. Leave real time for the drive to the airport, check-in, security and immigration.

items.title: Fill in the registration form, and add your flight details as soon as they are booked
items.body:
One form covers the whole event, so if you are attending both weeks you fill it in once. We use it to arrange visas, accommodation and airport pickups.

If you are travelling on a passport that does not get visa on arrival and you will need an invitation letter, say so on the form as early as you can. Those take time to arrange.

items.label: OBT-CDT Bali 2026 registration form
items.body: Airline, flight number, arrival and departure dates and times, and a mobile or WhatsApp number we can reach you on.

blocks.title: Airport transfers
blocks.body: We have budgeted to cover your transport between the airport and the base, and we arrange it from the flight details on the registration form. Getting yours in early is what lets us group arrivals so nobody waits long after landing.

items.title: Wait for a direct confirmation before you assume your pickup is booked
items.body: If your flight changes, tell us. We re-plan pickups around actual landing times, but only if we know about the change.

items.title: Driver details and pickup times
items.body: These go out closer to the date, once itineraries are in.

items.title: Worth doing while you are still at home

items.label: Check that the name on your ticket matches your passport exactly.
Keep passport, visa or entry approval, return ticket, insurance and accommodation details together and easy to reach.
Save offline copies of key documents and workshop contacts, and carry one on paper.
Tell the organisers promptly about itinerary changes, accessibility needs, allergies or medical needs.
Check baggage limits for every airline in your itinerary, including domestic and regional legs.
Carry essential medicines in their original packaging, with a prescription or doctor's letter where that helps.
Tell your bank you are travelling, and take more than one way to pay.
Travel day

items.label: Check before you travel

items.label: Passport

items.label: Visa

items.label: Onward travel
items.body: Carry evidence of a return or onward ticket in case it is asked for.

items.body: International tourists generally pay the Bali Tourism Levy of IDR 150,000 per person. Keep the voucher.
Use government portals only. Do not use agents, or links forwarded to you without checking where they go.

A refillable water bottle and a small day bag.

blocks.title: Meals and dietary needs
blocks.body:
Meals come through the base kitchen on working days. Part of what keeps the cost low enough for fifty people to attend is the generosity of our hosts, and one of the ways the base runs efficiently is by having large visiting groups help with meal preparation and cleanup.

We will organise that so those who are able-bodied share the work and it finishes quickly together, rather than anyone losing half an afternoon session to it.
blocks.caption: Nasi campur: rice with a ring of small dishes around it, the everyday shape of a meal in Bali.

items.title: Weekends
items.body: The base kitchen does not serve as many meals at the weekend, so we provide a meal stipend and you buy your own nearby. To be honest about the size of it: sensible rather than lavish, enough to eat well at places that follow normal food-safety practice.

items.title: Tell us about allergies and medically necessary dietary requirements, in writing
items.body: If you have not already done so, put it on the registration form or email it. An informal conversation is not something the kitchen can work from.

blocks.title: Participant preparation
blocks.body: The workshop is most fruitful when people arrive having already done the preparatory work. We consider it foundational: it shapes what you understand when you walk in, and how much help you can be to the translation teams. If you have hit obstacles, tell us. We would much rather talk it through than have you arrive feeling behind.

items.title: Exegesis of the two psalms
items.body: Study Psalm 1 first, then Psalm 13, using the Exegetical Guide. Psalm 1 is a wisdom psalm; Psalm 13 is a lament. The cohort schedule asked for Psalm 1 by 20 May and Psalm 13 by 8 June.

items.title: If you joined late
items.body: Do not try to recover the original dates. Start now and count from today: roughly two weeks on Psalm 1, then three on Psalm 13, with Hebrew reading practice running alongside in small amounts. If you are joining very close to the workshop, begin with Psalm 1 and ask us to help you prioritise the rest.

items.title: Hebrew reading fluency
items.body: Keep your Hebrew reading moving. Listening while following the Hebrew text is a good way to stay motivated and to get the rhythm of the poetry into your ear. The resources below were Katie's suggestions to the cohort.

items.title: Prepare your posture as well as your notes
items.body:
Pray for humility, attentiveness, creativity and a servant-hearted way of consulting. Come ready to learn from mother-tongue translators, from artists, from peers and from mentors, and expect feedback to change both your thinking and your work.

It also helps to notice, before you arrive, how poetry, song, lament, praise and wisdom already function in your own cultural setting.

blocks.title: Free time and exploring together
blocks.body:
Bali has a great deal to offer and you are warmly welcome to enjoy it. To be clear, the facilitators are not organising or sponsoring outings.

In past workshops participants decided together where they wanted to go, pooled money for a van, and went as a group. Some very good memories came out of that. We would love it to happen again, organised among yourselves.

workshops.title: Narrative
workshops.metaDescription: The first OBT-CDT workshop laid the foundations: OBT-specific exegesis, internalization, oral drafting, and introductory consulting awareness, practiced on biblical narrative.

blocks.title: Foundations, practiced on story
blocks.body:
Narrative came first for a reason: story is the Bible's most accessible genre and the natural on-ramp into oral translation work. The workshop built the foundational OBT skill set: exegesis with an oral lens, internalization of passages through embodied group activities, oral drafting and revision, and a first taste of what consultants listen for in a checking session.

Participants worked in teams through the full OBT cycle on narrative passages, with attention to the things that make or break an oral story: participant reference, story flow, and the storytelling conventions of oral cultures.

blocks.title: Who came
blocks.body:
Around twenty participants gathered in Bangalore from partner organizations across the region: field translators, exegetes, and translation advisors, many already serving active OBT projects. A three-person facilitation team led the two weeks, joined by consultants who provided checking feedback on the teams' work.

For most participants, this workshop was their first step onto the track, and the cohort that formed in Bangalore has continued together through everything since.

blocks.caption: Oral devotions and embodied internalization set the tone for the first workshop.

blocks.title: What it set in motion
blocks.body: Bangalore established the pattern every later workshop follows: teach only what cannot be gained from books, practice everything, and evaluate through observation rather than examination. It also confirmed the appetite: the interest that surfaced around this first workshop exceeded what one event could hold, and it shaped the plans for everything that followed.

blocks.title: The story continued in Chiang Mai

workshops.title: Epistles
workshops.metaDescription: The second OBT-CDT workshop tackled the Epistles: argument structure, discourse prominence, and the series' first mentored consultant checks on a real OBT translation.

blocks.title: From story to argument
blocks.body:
Epistles ask different questions of a translator than narrative does. Where a story lives on flow and participant reference, a letter lives on its argument: how each move builds on the last, where the emphasis falls, and what the writer is doing with every paragraph.

The second workshop equipped participants with genre-specific exegetical tools for the Epistles, centered on argument structure and discourse prominence, and put those tools to work on passages the teams translated and checked during the two weeks.

blocks.title: A real check, not a simulation
blocks.body:
The milestone of Chiang Mai was consulting practice with real stakes: participants took part in mentored consultant checking of an actual OBT Epistles translation, observed and guided by experienced consultants.

More than twenty consultants and consultants-in-training worked through the two weeks together, and each one left with a written evaluation grounded in what multiple facilitators had observed across the sessions.

blocks.caption: Teams mapping the argument structure of an epistle before drafting.

blocks.title: What followed
blocks.body:
After Chiang Mai, the track's between-workshop rhythm took shape: evaluation data from the workshop fed into a series of virtual trainings targeting the competencies participants most needed to strengthen before the Psalms workshop.

The workshop evaluations themselves flowed into each participant's competency record, reviewed with their mentors, adding another layer of documented evidence toward certification.

blocks.title: Psalms that sing in local voices
blocks.body:
The Psalms are poetry, and poetry refuses to travel as plain prose. This workshop trains consultants to exegete Hebrew poetry with an oral lens (imagery, parallelism, poetic structure, prominence) and to facilitate the translation of Psalms into the artistic genres a community already sings, chants, and performs.

The overarching framework is the Creating Local Arts Together (CLAT) process: discovering a community's own art forms, matching them to the purposes of a psalm, and creating translations that live as local worship.

blocks.kicker: The shape of the two weeks
blocks.title: From aesthetics to performance

items.title: Exegete, match, and craft
items.body: Aesthetic language and genre in the Psalms, Hebrew poetic conventions, and the CLAT process, applied immediately: teams study selected psalms, match them to local genres, and begin crafting them as local art with participating artists.

items.title: Check, revise, and integrate
items.body: Community and consultant checking of the crafted psalms, revision, supervised consulting practice on Psalms translated in minority languages, and integration conversations that plan how the songs live on in worship, ending with performances.

blocks.title: How participants are preparing
blocks.body:
Everyone arrives having already studied the psalms the workshop will translate and check. Prework covers basic Hebrew reading, the foundations of genre theory, the CLAT framework, and practice in crafting consultant checking questions, so the two weeks can be spent on formation rather than first exposure.

The teaching team brings together deep expertise in Hebrew poetry, ethnoarts, and OBT consulting.

The one-week experiential OBT Crash Course runs on the base from 18 to 22 August, immediately before the workshop, for participants who need those shared foundations first.

blocks.caption: Local artists and translation teams craft psalms in the community's own musical genres.
